Chushan-rishathaim
KOO-shan-rish-a-THAY-im
n. (proper, a king of Mesopotamia; Cushan of double wickedness)
Hebrew Kuwshan Rishathayim — Cushan with the dual ending of rishah, wickedness: Cushan of double wickedness. He is the first oppressor in the book of Judges, and the first deliverance in that book is from him.

Biblical Definition

The pattern of Judges is set by this king. “Therefore the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years” (Judges 3:8). Note who sold them: not a failure of Israel's defences but the anger of the LORD, and the oppressor is the instrument. Then the cry, and then the deliverer — Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother: “And the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war: and the LORD delivered Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand; and his hand prevailed against Chushanrishathaim” (Judges 3:10). Four elements appear here that will repeat through the book: Israel does evil, God sells them, Israel cries, God raises a deliverer on whom his Spirit comes. The name itself — double wickedness — is the sort of thing Hebrew narrative enjoys, and the land had rest forty years.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) has no entry for this proper name; Scripture fixes it as the king of Mesopotamia who oppressed Israel eight years and was delivered into the hand of Othniel.

expand to see more

MESOPOTAMIA, n. The country between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates; in Hebrew, Aram-naharaim, Syria of the two rivers.

OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity or rigor.

DELIVERER, n. One who delivers; one who releases or rescues; a preserver.

JUDGE, n. In the Hebrew commonwealth, a chief magistrate raised up by God to deliver and govern Israel.

CHASTISE, v.t. To correct by punishment; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender.

Key Scripture

Judges 3:8 — "Therefore the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years."

Judges 3:10 — "And the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war: and the LORD delivered Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand; and his hand prevailed against Chushanrishathaim."

Judges 3:9 — "And when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother."

Judges 3:11 — "And the land had rest forty years. And Othniel the son of Kenaz died."

Modern Corruption

Oppression is explained wholly by the strength and malice of the oppressor, where Judges 3 says the LORD sold Israel into his hand — and that the same LORD delivered him into Othniel's.

expand to see more

Judges 3:8 states a cause that no modern analysis would supply: the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he sold them. The oppressor was real, his power was real, and eight years of servitude were real; and the text puts the transaction in God's hands. This is not a denial that Chushan-rishathaim was wicked — his very name in the record is doubled wickedness — nor an excuse for him, since God judged him too. It is the refusal of a purely horizontal account of history. A nation that will not consider whether God is chastening it will learn nothing from its troubles.

The deliverance is described with equal care. Israel cried unto the LORD, and the LORD raised up a deliverer, and the Spirit of the LORD came upon him. Othniel did not volunteer, and his qualification is not his ability but the Spirit. The pattern holds through the book and through redemptive history: the people cry, God provides a deliverer of his own choosing and equipping, and the land has rest. Judges is the Old Testament's long argument that men cannot save themselves, told seven times over, and pointing beyond every judge to one Deliverer on whom the Spirit rested without measure.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Kuwshan Rishathayim (H3573), Cushan of double wickedness; Aram Naharayim (H763), Mesopotamia; makar (H4376), to sell; Othniyel (H6274), Othniel.

expand to see more

Hebrew Kuwshan Rishathayim (H3573) — Chushan-rishathaim; Cushan of double wickedness.

Hebrew rishah (H7564) — wickedness; doubled in the oppressor's very name.

Hebrew Aram Naharayim (H763) — Syria of the two rivers, Mesopotamia; his kingdom.

Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; the LORD sold Israel into his hand.

Hebrew Othniyel (H6274) — Othniel, lion of God; the first judge, Caleb's younger brother.

Usage

"“He sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim” — the stated cause."

"“The Spirit of the LORD came upon him” — the deliverer's qualification."

"“And the land had rest forty years” — the pattern completed."
